timeline.name: Coup against Prime Minister Mossadegh
timeline.line: US- and UK-backed coup removes Mossadegh after oil nationalization
timeline.description: After Iran nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, a CIA- and MI6-supported operation restored the Shah's authority. The CIA acknowledged its role in documents released in 2013.
timeline.immediate_effect: Shah consolidated power; oil consortium with Western majors.
timeline.long_term_effect: A documented grievance central to the Islamic Republic's narrative of foreign interference.

timeline.name: Iranian Revolution and embassy seizure
timeline.line: Revolution replaces the monarchy; US embassy seized in November
timeline.description: The Pahlavi monarchy fell in February 1979; the Islamic Republic was proclaimed in April; the US embassy was seized on 4 November and 52 hostages held for 444 days.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rupture of US-Iran relations that has never been repaired.
timeline.long_term_effect: Sanctions architecture, US regional basing and Iran's 'resistance' posture all descend from this break.

timeline.name: Carter Doctrine
timeline.line: US declares any attempt to control the Gulf an assault on its vital interests, to be repelled by force
timeline.description: Announced in the State of the Union after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iranian revolution. The basis for CENTCOM and the permanent US naval presence.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rapid Deployment Force created.
timeline.long_term_effect: Documented doctrine that still frames US responses to Hormuz threats.

timeline.name: Iran-Iraq War
timeline.line: Eight-year war with Iraq, including the Tanker War in the Gulf
timeline.description: Iraq invaded in September 1980; the war settled into attrition with chemical weapons use by Iraq and missile strikes on cities. Iran accepted UNSCR 598 in July 1988.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hundreds of thousands dead; no border change.
timeline.long_term_effect: Iran's missile program, self-reliance doctrine and distrust of international institutions (which did not condemn Iraq's chemical use forcefully) are commonly traced to this war.

timeline.name: Tanker War
timeline.line: Tanker War: hundreds of ships attacked; US reflags Kuwaiti tankers and destroys Iranian platforms
timeline.description: Iraq attacked Iranian tankers and Kharg Island; Iran retaliated against Gulf Arab shipping. The US reflagged Kuwaiti tankers (Operation Earnest Will, 1987) and, after USS Samuel B. Roberts hit a mine, destroyed Iranian oil platforms and naval units (Operation Praying Mantis, April 1988). USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air 655 in July 1988. The strait was never closed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran's conventional navy was badly damaged; Iran accepted a ceasefire weeks later.
timeline.long_term_effect: The origin of the IRGC Navy's asymmetric small-boat and mine doctrine, and of the US pattern of escorting shipping rather than striking Iran proper.

timeline.name: Closure threats during the 2011-12 sanctions escalation
timeline.line: Iran threatens to close the strait if oil sanctions bite; exercises follow; no closure
timeline.description: As the EU oil embargo and US financial sanctions were adopted, Iranian officials said not a drop of oil would pass; Iran held naval exercises and the US sent carriers. Traffic continued.
timeline.immediate_effect: Oil price premium; no interdiction.
timeline.long_term_effect: Established that closure threats are a bargaining signal that has not been executed.

timeline.name: Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action
timeline.line: JCPOA caps enrichment for sanctions relief; endorsed by UNSCR 2231
timeline.description: Iran accepted limits on enrichment and stockpiles with IAEA verification in exchange for lifting nuclear-related sanctions.
timeline.problem_solved: Iranian breakout time under a year.
timeline.did_it_survive: The US withdrew in May 2018; Iran exceeded the limits from 2019 and had enriched to 60 percent by 2021; the deal was moribund by 2025.

timeline.name: US withdraws from the JCPOA; 'maximum pressure'
timeline.line: US exits the deal and reimposes sanctions; the 2019 Gulf incidents follow within a year
timeline.description: The US reimposed and expanded sanctions, driving Iranian oil exports down sharply in 2019.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iranian economy contracted; Iran began exceeding JCPOA limits in 2019.
timeline.long_term_effect: The precedent Iranian negotiators cite for demanding guarantees against future US reversals.

timeline.name: 2019 tanker attacks, drone shoot-down and seizures
timeline.line: Limpet-mine attacks on tankers, an RQ-4 shot down, the Stena Impero seized; no closure
timeline.description: Attacks on tankers off Fujairah (May) and in the Gulf of Oman (June) attributed by the US to Iran; Iran shot down a US RQ-4 on 20 June and the US called off a retaliatory strike; the IRGC seized the British-flagged Stena Impero on 19 July after the UK detained an Iranian tanker at Gibraltar. Both ships were released by late September.
timeline.immediate_effect: Insurance premiums rose; coalition escort missions formed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed Iran's preference for deniable, reversible actions against shipping and the US preference for avoiding direct strikes on Iran.

timeline.name: Attack on Saudi Abqaiq and Khurais facilities
timeline.line: Drone and missile strike halves Saudi output for days; Houthis claim it, US and Saudi Arabia blame Iran
timeline.description: The largest single disruption of oil supply in history by volume, for a short period. Attribution to Iranian territory was asserted by the US and Saudi Arabia; Iran denied it; the Houthis claimed it.
timeline.immediate_effect: Brief oil price spike; no US military response.
timeline.long_term_effect: Demonstrated that Gulf energy can be hit without touching the strait.

timeline.name: US strike kills Qasem Soleimani; Iran strikes Al Asad
timeline.line: US kills Soleimani; Iran fires missiles at US bases in Iraq with advance warning; both sides stop
timeline.description: Iran's 8 January ballistic-missile strike on Al Asad and Erbil was preceded by warning through Iraq; no US personnel were killed and the US did not respond. Iran then mistakenly shot down flight PS752.
timeline.immediate_effect: De-escalation within a week.
timeline.long_term_effect: The clearest documented case of Iranian retaliation calibrated to avoid war.

timeline.name: 2023 tanker seizures (Advantage Sweet, Niovi)
timeline.line: Iran seizes two tankers in a week; the US adds naval assets; traffic continues
timeline.description: Seizures followed US confiscation of Iranian oil cargoes under sanctions. The US announced additional F-35s, F-16s and a destroyer to the region in the following months.
timeline.immediate_effect: Tit-for-tat cargo seizures.
timeline.long_term_effect: Confirmed the seizure-for-seizure pattern.

timeline.name: First direct Iran-Israel strikes
timeline.line: Iran fires drones and missiles at Israel in April and October 2024; Israel strikes Iranian air defenses
timeline.description: After Israel struck Iran's consulate in Damascus on 1 April, Iran launched roughly 300 drones and missiles on 13-14 April, mostly intercepted with US and allied help; a second, larger ballistic strike followed on 1 October after the killing of Hezbollah's leader; Israel struck Iranian air defenses and missile production on 26 October.
timeline.immediate_effect: The shadow war became direct; the strait was not affected.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set the escalation ladder that the June 2025 war climbed.

timeline.name: June 2025 Israel-Iran war and Majlis closure vote
timeline.line: Israel and then the US strike Iran's nuclear sites; parliament votes to close Hormuz; the strait stays open and a ceasefire follows
timeline.description: Israel opened a campaign against Iranian nuclear and military targets on 13 June; the US struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan on 22 June; Iran's parliament voted the same day to close the strait, a decision left to the Supreme National Security Council and not executed; Iran fired a telegraphed salvo at Al Udeid on 23 June; a ceasefire took hold on 24 June.
timeline.immediate_effect: Twelve-day war; oil rose then fell back when the strait stayed open.
timeline.long_term_effect: Even under direct attack on its nuclear program, Iran did not close the strait; the strongest data point yet for the not_implemented pattern, and also a data point for how far escalation can go without closure.

lessons.name: US: Gulf access is a vital interest to be defended by force
lessons.description: Stated in the 1980 State of the Union and never rescinded; the institutional expression is CENTCOM and Fifth Fleet.

lessons.name: Iran: no outside power will protect it, so build missiles and asymmetric naval forces
lessons.description: Widely attributed by analysts to the Iran-Iraq War experience of missile attacks on cities and muted international response to chemical weapons. Iranian officials invoke the war constantly, so the linkage is well supported, but the doctrine is not laid out in a single public document.

lessons.name: Iran uses the strait as a threat it cannot afford to execute
lessons.description: Inference from the historical record (no closure in any crisis) and from Iran's export dependence on the same waterway. A regime facing existential defeat could still act against its economic interest; the inference weakens as Iran's stake in the strait's traffic falls.

tendencies.name: Iran retaliates in ways that are visible, deniable or telegraphed, and stop short of war with the US
contradicting: The 1984-88 Tanker War escalated to direct US-Iran naval combat; the 2019 Abqaiq attack, if Iranian, was a major unclaimed strike on a US partner; the October 2024 salvo was larger and less telegraphed than April's.
current_evidence: The June 2025 Al Udeid strike was announced in advance through Qatar and caused no casualties.
tendencies.caveat: Calibration has held while the regime's survival was not at stake. The June 2025 strikes on nuclear sites are the closest test so far, and the regime still calibrated; a leadership succession or an internal crisis could change the calculus.

path_dependencies.name: From 1979 to export dependence on China through the same strait

chain.step: 1979 revolution and hostage crisis break US-Iran relations
Sanctions regimes accumulate (1979, 1995, 2006-10 UN, 2012 EU, 2018 US)
Iran's oil exports narrow to a small set of buyers, mostly China, shipped through Hormuz
Current constraint: closing the strait would cut Iran's main revenue; threatening it remains cheap

path_dependencies.description: Documented sanctions and trade data; the constraint on Iranian behaviour is an assessment.

narratives.name: Iran: a century of foreign interference justifies resistance and self-reliance
narratives.modern_interpretation: The Islamic Republic frames its foreign policy as resistance to US and Israeli domination. The 1953 coup is documented; the claim that current US policy continues it is a political interpretation.

narratives.name: US: Iran as a hostage-taking, terror-sponsoring regime since 1979
narratives.modern_interpretation: Frames US policy across administrations and constrains any president's room to normalize relations. The events are documented; the framing is a domestic political narrative.

cases.name: Closure threats during the 2011-12 sanctions escalation
2019 tanker attacks, drone shoot-down and seizures
June 2025 Israel-Iran war and Majlis closure vote

hormuz_disruption.selection_note: Cases are episodes in which Iran threatened, attacked or seized shipping in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Outcome 'limited_conflict' means attacks or seizures occurred without closure; 'not_implemented' means a closure threat was not acted on. No case in the record involves an actual sustained closure, which is the base rate the analyst should start from and then update with Iran's present dependence on the strait for its own exports.
hormuz_disruption.note: only 5 comparable cases: use as a rough prior, not a percentage

timeline.name: Japan annexes Korea
timeline.line: Japan annexes Korea; 35 years of colonial rule
timeline.description: The annexation treaty ended Korean sovereignty until 1945.
timeline.immediate_effect: Colonial administration and industrialization concentrated in the north.
timeline.long_term_effect: Colonial-era grievances (forced labour, 'comfort women') still drive ROK-Japan relations and complicate trilateral security cooperation.

timeline.name: Korea divided at the 38th parallel
timeline.line: US and Soviet occupation zones split the peninsula; two states follow in 1948
timeline.description: A line chosen hastily in Washington for accepting the Japanese surrender became the boundary between rival states proclaimed in August and September 1948.
timeline.immediate_effect: Two governments each claiming the whole peninsula.
timeline.long_term_effect: The division is the root of every subsequent crisis.

timeline.name: Korean War
timeline.line: North Korea invades; UN forces and then China intervene; armistice restores roughly the original line
timeline.description: The North's June 1950 invasion nearly took the whole peninsula; the UN counteroffensive reached the Yalu; Chinese intervention pushed the front back to near the 38th parallel where it stalemated.
timeline.immediate_effect: Millions dead; the peninsula devastated.
timeline.long_term_effect: Permanent US troop presence in the South, the PRC-DPRK bond, and the North's siege identity.

timeline.name: Korean Armistice Agreement
timeline.line: Armistice halts the fighting; no peace treaty has ever followed
timeline.description: Signed by the UNC, the KPA and the Chinese People's Volunteers; the ROK did not sign. Established the DMZ and the Military Armistice Commission.
timeline.did_it_survive: In force for seven decades, with repeated DPRK declarations that it no longer recognizes it; no peace treaty.

timeline.name: US-ROK Mutual Defense Treaty
timeline.line: US-ROK alliance treaty; US forces stationed in Korea ever since
timeline.description: Each party would act to meet a common danger in accordance with constitutional processes; the basis for US Forces Korea, about 28,500 personnel.
timeline.problem_solved: Reassuring Seoul against a renewed invasion and restraining it from unilateral action.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, through repeated crises and burden-sharing disputes.

timeline.name: PRC-DPRK Treaty of Friendship, Co-operation and Mutual Assistance
timeline.line: China's only formal mutual-assistance treaty, still in force
timeline.description: Article 2 commits each side to immediate military and other assistance if the other is attacked.
timeline.did_it_survive: Renewed in 1981 and 2001; Beijing's reading of the automaticity of Article 2 is deliberately ambiguous.

timeline.name: Blue House raid and USS Pueblo seizure
timeline.description: A commando team attempted to assassinate President Park; two days later the DPRK seized USS Pueblo. Dozens killed in the raid and its pursuit; the Pueblo crew was released after eleven months of negotiation.

timeline.name: Panmunjom axe murder incident
timeline.description: Two US officers killed in the Joint Security Area; the US responded with a massive show of force to cut the tree (Operation Paul Bunyan) and Kim Il Sung expressed regret.

timeline.name: Rangoon bombing
timeline.description: DPRK agents bombed a ceremony in Rangoon, killing 21 including four ROK cabinet ministers; Burma severed relations; no ROK military retaliation.

timeline.name: US-DPRK Agreed Framework
timeline.line: Agreed Framework freezes the plutonium program in exchange for reactors and fuel; collapses in 2002
timeline.description: The DPRK froze its Yongbyon reactors in return for light-water reactors and heavy fuel oil.
timeline.problem_solved: The 1994 crisis in which the US considered strikes on Yongbyon.
timeline.did_it_survive: Collapsed in 2002 over a suspected uranium program; the DPRK withdrew from the NPT in 2003 and tested in 2006.

timeline.name: First North Korean nuclear test
timeline.line: First nuclear test; UN sanctions begin
timeline.description: UNSCR 1718 followed within days; five more tests followed through 2017.
timeline.immediate_effect: Sanctions regime established.
timeline.long_term_effect: Denuclearization became the frame for all subsequent diplomacy, and then an unrealistic one.

timeline.name: Sinking of ROKS Cheonan
timeline.line: ROKS Cheonan sunk by a North Korean torpedo, 46 sailors killed; Seoul responds with sanctions, not force
timeline.description: The multinational investigation attributed the sinking to a DPRK torpedo; Pyongyang denies it. The ROK imposed the May 24 measures suspending most inter-Korean trade.

timeline.name: Shelling of Yeonpyeong Island
timeline.line: North Korean artillery shells Yeonpyeong; the ROK returns fire; four killed
timeline.description: The first artillery attack on ROK territory since 1953, during an ROK live-fire drill. The ROK fired back and later changed rules of engagement to allow disproportionate response.

timeline.name: DMZ landmine maiming and artillery exchange
timeline.description: Two ROK soldiers maimed by mines; the ROK resumed loudspeaker broadcasts; an artillery exchange followed on 20 August; a 25 August agreement ended the standoff with a DPRK expression of regret.

timeline.name: 2017 thermonuclear test and ICBM launches
timeline.line: Sixth nuclear test and first ICBMs able to reach the US mainland; 'fire and fury' rhetoric; then a pivot to summits
timeline.description: The September 2017 test was assessed as thermonuclear; the Hwasong-15 launch in November demonstrated intercontinental range. UNSCR 2397 followed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Peak sanctions and war talk.
timeline.long_term_effect: Kim declared the nuclear force 'complete' and moved to diplomacy from a position of demonstrated capability.

timeline.name: Singapore and Hanoi summits
timeline.line: First US-DPRK leaders' summit; Hanoi collapses over sanctions relief for Yongbyon
timeline.description: The Singapore statement committed to 'work toward complete denuclearization' without a definition; Hanoi ended without agreement when the US rejected Yongbyon-for-major-sanctions-relief.
timeline.immediate_effect: Test moratorium 2018-2021.
timeline.long_term_effect: Kim concluded that diplomacy on those terms would not deliver; the 2022 law followed.

timeline.name: DPRK law declaring nuclear status irreversible
timeline.line: Law states the nuclear status is irreversible and authorizes preemptive use if the leadership is threatened
timeline.description: Codified conditions for nuclear use, including a decapitation attempt, and ruled out denuclearization as a negotiating subject.
timeline.immediate_effect: Denuclearization talks foreclosed by DPRK law.
timeline.long_term_effect: The documented doctrine against which any future DPRK offer should be read.

timeline.name: Kim abandons unification; ROK designated the principal enemy
timeline.line: Kim declares the two Koreas separate hostile states and orders unification institutions dismantled
timeline.description: A break with the unification framework maintained since 1948; inter-Korean agencies were abolished and the constitution ordered amended.
timeline.immediate_effect: Inter-Korean channels closed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Removes the 'one nation' restraint on the use of force against the South, in Pyongyang's own framing. Whether behaviour follows the framing is an open question.

timeline.name: DPRK-Russia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty
timeline.line: Putin and Kim sign a mutual-assistance treaty; North Korean troops fight in Kursk within months
timeline.description: Article 4 provides for military and other assistance if either is attacked. The ROK NIS and the US assessed in October 2024 that thousands of DPRK troops had deployed to Russia; Pyongyang acknowledged the deployment in April 2025.
timeline.problem_solved: Russia's munitions and manpower shortfall; DPRK's isolation and technology needs.
timeline.did_it_survive: In force and operationalized within four months, which is faster than most alliances are tested.

territories.name: Northern Limit Line and the West Sea islands

historical_control.note: line drawn unilaterally by the UNC after the armistice; the five islands are ROK-administered

current_claims.basis: de facto boundary since 1953
rejects the NLL; proposed its own line in 1999 and 2007

territories.recognition: The armistice does not define a maritime boundary; the NLL has no treaty basis but has functioned as the line for seven decades.
significance: military (site of the 1999, 2002, 2009 naval clashes and the 2010 Yeonpyeong shelling)

lessons.name: ROK: security rests on the US alliance and combined deterrence
lessons.description: Stated in every ROK defense white paper; institutionalized in the Combined Forces Command and extended-deterrence consultations (Washington Declaration, 2023).

lessons.name: DPRK: nuclear weapons guarantee regime survival and are not negotiable
lessons.description: Written into the 2022 nuclear forces law and the 2023 constitutional amendment. The regime cites Iraq and Libya as what happens to states that disarm; that inference is the regime's own stated reasoning.

lessons.name: China: prevent a US-aligned unified Korea on the Yalu
lessons.description: The standard reading of China's 1950 intervention and continued support for Pyongyang despite nuclear tests. Chinese documents describe 'peace and stability' priorities; the buffer logic is inferred by analysts and by Chinese scholars, not stated as doctrine.

tendencies.name: North Korea alternates lethal or nuclear provocation with offers to talk, keeping each below the threshold of war
contradicting: Since 2019 the DPRK has refused talks entirely and in 2024 renounced unification, so the bargaining half of the cycle has not recurred under Kim Jong Un's later period; the 1950 invasion itself is the case where provocation was war.
current_evidence: Russia now supplies what bargaining with Washington used to: the incentive to return to the cycle is weaker than at any point since 1991.
tendencies.caveat: The cycle was a product of isolation. With Russian backing the regime may not need it, so the historical pattern may be less predictive now than at any time since it was identified.

path_dependencies.name: From an armistice without a peace treaty to a nuclear-armed 'two hostile states'

chain.step: 1953 armistice leaves a legal state of war and a UNC presence
US-ROK treaty stations US forces permanently
Pyongyang frames the US presence as a 'hostile policy' justifying a deterrent
Nuclear status written into law (2022) and constitution (2023)
Current constraint: denuclearization is legally foreclosed by the DPRK and politically required by the US and ROK; there is no overlap to negotiate in

path_dependencies.description: Documents at each step; the causal arrows are assessments.

narratives.name: DPRK: a besieged fortress facing a US hostile policy since 1950
narratives.historical_event: 1950-53 war and US bombing; sanctions since 2006
narratives.modern_interpretation: State media frames every sanction and exercise as continuation of the war. The bombing campaign is documented; the claim of unbroken US intent to destroy the state is regime narrative.

narratives.name: ROK: peaceful unification as constitutional duty
narratives.modern_interpretation: Article 4 of the ROK constitution mandates pursuit of peaceful unification; policy oscillates between engagement and pressure by administration. The 2024 DPRK renunciation left the ROK narrative without a counterpart.

The set is not exhaustive of every DMZ incident, only of the well-documented lethal ones, so it is a floor on frequency and a fair sample of outcomes.

timeline.name: Pereiaslav Agreement
timeline.line: Cossack Hetmanate swears allegiance to the Tsar: the origin point of rival 'unity' and 'subjugation' narratives
timeline.description: Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossacks accepted the protection of the Muscovite Tsar. Russian imperial and Soviet historiography read it as 'reunification'; Ukrainian historiography reads it as a military alliance later violated.
timeline.immediate_effect: Muscovite expansion into left-bank Ukraine.
timeline.long_term_effect: The dueling readings are the seed of the historical-unity narrative Putin invoked in 2021.

timeline.name: Ukrainian SSR becomes a founding republic of the USSR
timeline.line: Ukraine enters the USSR as a republic with formal borders that became its 1991 state borders
timeline.description: After the 1917-21 wars the Ukrainian SSR joined the union as a constituent republic. Its administrative borders, expanded in 1939-45 and 1954, became international borders in 1991.
timeline.immediate_effect: Ukrainian statehood existed on paper inside the union.
timeline.long_term_effect: Putin's 2022 address blamed Lenin for 'creating' Ukraine, showing the border origin is itself contested.

timeline.name: Holodomor famine
timeline.line: Famine kills millions in Soviet Ukraine; recognized by Ukraine as genocide, disputed by Russia
timeline.description: Millions died in the 1932-33 famine in Ukraine under Soviet grain requisition. Ukraine's parliament recognized it as genocide in 2006; Russia rejects that characterization.
timeline.immediate_effect: Demographic catastrophe.
timeline.long_term_effect: Central to modern Ukrainian national memory; a documented divergence between Russian and Ukrainian official narratives.

timeline.name: Crimea transferred from the RSFSR to the Ukrainian SSR
timeline.line: Soviet decree moves Crimea to the Ukrainian SSR
timeline.description: An internal Soviet administrative transfer. It became an international border in 1991 and is cited by Russia as an 'error' to be reversed.
timeline.immediate_effect: None internationally at the time.
timeline.long_term_effect: The origin of Crimea being Ukrainian in 1991; the 2014 seizure reversed it by force.

timeline.name: Egyptian mobilization into Sinai, May 1967
timeline.description: Egypt moved forces into Sinai, expelled UNEF and closed the Straits of Tiran; Israel struck first on 5 June.

timeline.name: Egyptian and Syrian mobilization under exercise cover, October 1973
timeline.description: Repeated exercises had desensitized Israeli intelligence; the real attack came on 6 October.

timeline.name: Iraqi buildup on the Kuwaiti border, July 1990
timeline.description: Iraq massed roughly 100,000 troops; most governments assessed coercion over oil quotas and debt; Iraq invaded on 2 August.

timeline.name: Ukraine independence referendum
timeline.line: Ukraine votes for independence, with a majority in every region including Crimea
timeline.description: About 90 percent voted for independence on high turnout; Crimea recorded a majority in favour (roughly 54 percent). The USSR dissolved weeks later.
timeline.immediate_effect: Ukraine became a sovereign state within its Soviet-era borders.
timeline.long_term_effect: The referendum is Ukraine's primary answer to claims that its borders are artificial.

timeline.name: Budapest Memorandum
timeline.line: Ukraine gives up the Soviet nuclear arsenal for security assurances from Russia, the US and the UK
timeline.description: Ukraine acceded to the NPT and transferred the warheads on its territory to Russia; the three powers reaffirmed commitments to respect Ukraine's borders and refrain from threat or use of force. The document is a political memorandum, not a defense treaty.
timeline.did_it_survive: Violated by Russia in 2014; the US and UK gave no security guarantee and responded with sanctions and aid rather than force.

timeline.name: Russia-Ukraine Treaty of Friendship and Black Sea Fleet agreements
timeline.line: Russia recognizes Ukraine's borders and leases Sevastopol for the fleet until 2017
timeline.description: Russia recognized Ukraine's existing borders and the two states divided the Black Sea Fleet, with Russia leasing bases in Sevastopol to 2017.
timeline.did_it_survive: The lease was extended in 2010; Ukraine terminated the friendship treaty in 2019 after the 2014 seizure of Crimea.

timeline.name: India's Operation Parakram
timeline.description: Ten-month full mobilization after the attack on India's parliament; no war under nuclear shadow; stood down in October 2002.

timeline.name: Orange Revolution
timeline.line: Mass protests overturn a rigged election; the Moscow-backed candidate loses the rerun
timeline.description: Protests against fraud in the 2004 presidential runoff led to a court-ordered rerun won by Viktor Yushchenko over the Kremlin-favoured Viktor Yanukovych.
timeline.immediate_effect: Westward-leaning government in Kyiv.
timeline.long_term_effect: Read in Moscow as Western-engineered regime change; a template for the 2014 reaction.

timeline.name: NATO Bucharest summit declaration on Ukraine and Georgia
timeline.line: NATO declares Ukraine and Georgia 'will become members' but grants no Membership Action Plan
timeline.description: Paragraph 23 of the declaration promised eventual membership while withholding a MAP. Putin, attending, warned against it.
timeline.immediate_effect: Neither deterrence nor reassurance: a promise without a timetable.
timeline.long_term_effect: Cited by Moscow as evidence of encirclement and by critics of NATO as the worst of both worlds; Russia used force in Georgia four months later.

timeline.name: Russia-Georgia war
timeline.line: Russia fights a five-day war with Georgia after large exercises on the border
timeline.description: Russian forces massed for the Kavkaz-2008 exercise in July; after Georgian shelling of Tskhinvali on 7 August, Russia invaded and recognized South Ossetia and Abkhazia. The EU fact-finding mission found Georgia started the shooting and Russia's response exceeded self-defense.
timeline.immediate_effect: Two Georgian regions under Russian protection.
timeline.long_term_effect: First post-Soviet use of Russian regular forces to change a neighbour's borders; the West's limited response is often read as a signal Moscow drew on in 2014.

timeline.name: Kharkiv Pact extends the Sevastopol lease to 2042
timeline.line: Yanukovych extends Russia's fleet lease to 2042 for a gas discount
timeline.description: Ukraine extended the Black Sea Fleet lease by 25 years in exchange for lower gas prices.
timeline.immediate_effect: Russian fleet presence in Crimea locked in.
timeline.long_term_effect: Forces already legally based in Crimea in 2014 made the seizure fast and nearly bloodless.

timeline.name: Euromaidan and the fall of Yanukovych
timeline.line: Euromaidan protests topple Yanukovych after he abandons the EU association agreement
timeline.description: Months of protest following the suspension of the EU association agreement ended with dozens killed and the president fleeing to Russia.
timeline.immediate_effect: Pro-Western interim government; Moscow called it a coup.
timeline.long_term_effect: The immediate trigger for the seizure of Crimea and the Donbas war.

timeline.name: Seizure of Crimea and outbreak of the Donbas war
timeline.line: Unmarked Russian troops seize Crimea; Russia annexes it and war begins in Donbas
timeline.description: Russian forces without insignia took control of Crimea from 27 February; a referendum on 16 March and accession treaty on 18 March followed. Tens of thousands of Russian troops massed on the eastern border while armed separatists, then Russian regulars, fought in Donetsk and Luhansk.
timeline.immediate_effect: Crimea annexed; roughly a third of Donbas under separatist control; sanctions.
timeline.long_term_effect: A frozen-then-hot conflict that the 2015 Minsk settlement never resolved.

timeline.name: Downing of flight MH17
timeline.line: MH17 shot down over Donbas by a Russian Buk system, per the Joint Investigation Team
timeline.description: 298 killed. The JIT concluded the Buk came from Russia's 53rd Brigade; a Dutch court convicted three men in absentia in 2022. Russia denies involvement.
timeline.immediate_effect: EU sectoral sanctions.
timeline.long_term_effect: Locked Western sanctions in place and hardened opinion.

timeline.name: Minsk II (Package of Measures)
timeline.line: Minsk II ceasefire and political package, endorsed by the UN Security Council; never implemented
timeline.description: Ceasefire, heavy-weapons withdrawal, special status and elections for the separatist areas, and Ukrainian control of the border only after elections. The sequencing dispute was never resolved.
timeline.did_it_survive: Reduced but never ended the fighting; Russia declared it dead in February 2022 by recognizing the separatist entities.

timeline.name: Doklam standoff
timeline.description: Ten-week face-off over Chinese road construction on the Bhutan-China border; mutual disengagement without shots fired.

timeline.name: Russian spring 2021 buildup on Ukraine's border
timeline.line: Around 100,000 Russian troops mass on the border, then partially withdraw
timeline.description: The largest concentration since 2014; Russia announced a pullback on 22 April but left equipment in place. The Biden-Putin Geneva summit followed in June.
timeline.immediate_effect: No attack; equipment pre-positioned.
timeline.long_term_effect: Later read as a rehearsal or a test of Western reaction; at the time it was read by many as coercive signalling, which is why the winter buildup was discounted.

timeline.name: Putin's essay 'On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians'
timeline.line: Putin publishes an essay denying Ukraine's separate nationhood, seven months before the invasion
timeline.description: The essay argued Russians and Ukrainians are one people and Ukraine's current form is a Western project. It was distributed to Russian troops.
timeline.immediate_effect: Public statement of intent that many analysts discounted.
timeline.long_term_effect: Evidence that stated historical narrative preceded and accompanied action, relevant to weighing future statements.

timeline.name: Winter 2021-22 buildup and full-scale invasion
timeline.line: After a months-long buildup, Russia recognizes the separatist republics and invades on 24 February 2022
timeline.description: US intelligence publicly warned of invasion from November 2021; Russia denied it. On 21 February Putin recognized the DNR and LNR, and on 24 February launched a multi-axis invasion including a thrust at Kyiv that failed by April. UNGA ES-11/1 condemned the aggression with 141 votes.
timeline.immediate_effect: Largest war in Europe since 1945; unprecedented sanctions; NATO enlargement to Finland and Sweden.
timeline.long_term_effect: Ongoing; the settlement terms will define the region's borders and security architecture.

timeline.name: Black Sea Grain Initiative and its termination
timeline.line: UN- and Turkey-brokered grain corridor operates for a year; Russia withdraws in July 2023
timeline.description: Allowed Ukrainian grain exports from Odesa-area ports; Russia withdrew citing unmet demands on its own exports. Ukraine subsequently opened its own corridor under naval-drone cover.
timeline.immediate_effect: Global food price relief, then renewed risk.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed a narrow deal can survive active war for a limited time and that Ukraine could contest the Black Sea without a navy.

timeline.name: Russia claims annexation of four Ukrainian oblasts
timeline.line: Russia proclaims annexation of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson; UNGA rejects it 143-5
timeline.description: After staged referendums Russia amended its constitution to include the four oblasts, none of which it fully controlled.
timeline.immediate_effect: Any ceasefire now involves territory Russia's constitution calls Russian.
timeline.long_term_effect: A constitutional lock-in that raises the domestic cost of Russian concessions.

timeline.name: DPRK-Russia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty
timeline.line: Putin and Kim sign a mutual-assistance treaty; North Korean troops fight in Kursk within months
timeline.description: Article 4 provides for military and other assistance if either is attacked. The ROK NIS and the US assessed in October 2024 that thousands of DPRK troops had deployed to Russia; Pyongyang acknowledged the deployment in April 2025.
timeline.problem_solved: Russia's munitions and manpower shortfall; DPRK's isolation and technology needs.
timeline.did_it_survive: In force and operationalized within four months, which is faster than most alliances are tested.

timeline.name: Ukrainian incursion into Kursk oblast
timeline.line: Ukraine seizes a pocket of Russian territory in Kursk; Russia retakes it by spring 2025 with North Korean troops
timeline.description: The first foreign occupation of Russian territory since 1945, held for roughly eight months.
timeline.immediate_effect: Russian redeployments; North Korean troops committed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Demonstrated the DPRK-Russia treaty in practice.

timeline.name: Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage
timeline.line: First US-Russia leaders' meeting since the invasion; no ceasefire agreed
timeline.description: The meeting produced no signed agreement; subsequent diplomacy focused on security guarantees for Ukraine and territorial questions.
timeline.immediate_effect: Re-opened direct US-Russia channel.
timeline.long_term_effect: Unknown; record here ends and the daily brief carries the current state.

territories.name: Crimea

current_claims.basis: 1991 borders; UNGA 68/262
March 2014 referendum and accession treaty, not recognized by the UNGA majority

territories.recognition: UNGA 68/262 (100 in favour, 11 against, 58 abstaining) affirmed Ukraine's territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.
significance: military (Sevastopol, Black Sea Fleet home port)
strategic geography (Black Sea access, Kerch Strait)

territories.name: Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts (Donbas)

historical_control.note: parts held by Russian-backed forces from 2014 and by Russia from 2022

current_claims.basis: 1991 borders
September 2022 claimed annexation, rejected by UNGA ES-11/4

territories.recognition: UNGA ES-11/4 (143 in favour) declared the 2022 annexation attempts invalid.
territories.de_facto_control: divided; majority under Russian control as of 2025
significance: ethnolinguistic (large Russian-speaking population used as justification)

lessons.name: Russia: keep neighbours out of hostile alliances
lessons.description: Russian security documents describe NATO enlargement as a threat and the 'near abroad' as a zone of privileged interest (Medvedev, 2008). That NATO enlargement causally drove the 2022 invasion is an interpretation contested between scholars; the documented fact is that Moscow states it as a grievance.

lessons.name: Ukraine: political assurances without guarantees do not deter
lessons.description: Ukrainian leaders cite the Budapest Memorandum's failure as the reason they demand binding guarantees or NATO membership in any settlement. The lesson is stated by Ukrainian officials; its generalization to other cases is inference.

lessons.name: Limited Western responses in 2008 and 2014 lowered Moscow's expected cost in 2022
lessons.description: An inference frequently made by analysts and impossible to verify against Kremlin decision records. It should not be presented as a demonstrated causal chain.

tendencies.name: Russia uses force when a neighbour's alignment shifts westward and Moscow judges the cost acceptable
contradicting: Baltic states joined NATO in 2004 with no Russian military response; Finland and Sweden joined in 2023-24 without one; the 2021 spring buildup ended in withdrawal.
current_evidence: The 2022 war continues; Russia has not opened a second front against a NATO member.
tendencies.caveat: The pattern holds for non-NATO neighbours only; membership appears to change the calculation, which is itself the argument for and against enlargement.

path_dependencies.name: From a 1954 administrative decree to a constitutional lock-in

chain.step: 1954: Crimea moved to the Ukrainian SSR inside one state
1991: internal line becomes an international border with a Russian fleet inside it
1997/2010: fleet lease keeps Russian forces in Sevastopol
2014: forces already in place seize the peninsula in days
2022: Russia writes four more oblasts into its constitution
Current constraint: any settlement must handle territory both constitutions claim

path_dependencies.description: Each arrow is a hypothesis; the decree, treaties and constitutional amendments are documented.

narratives.name: Russia: Russians and Ukrainians are one people; Ukraine is an anti-Russia project
narratives.modern_interpretation: Putin's 2021 essay and 2022 addresses present Ukrainian statehood as a Bolshevik and Western artefact. The narrative is documented in primary texts; it is a political interpretation, not a historical finding.

narratives.name: Ukraine: a centuries-long struggle for statehood against Russian domination
narratives.modern_interpretation: Official commemoration frames the current war as the continuation of a liberation struggle. The events are documented; the continuity claim is a narrative.

cases.name: Egyptian and Syrian mobilization under exercise cover, October 1973
Iraqi buildup on the Kuwaiti border, July 1990
Seizure of Crimea and outbreak of the Donbas war
Russian spring 2021 buildup on Ukraine's border

border_mobilization.selection_note: Cases are large, visible troop concentrations on a neighbour's border. The set is drawn from well-documented crises and is biased toward mobilizations that became famous because they led to war; quiet buildups that dissolved are under-recorded. Treat the war share as an upper bound on the prior, not a point estimate.

timeline.name: Spain cedes the Philippines to the United States (Treaty of Paris)
timeline.line: Spain cedes the Philippines to the US inside lines that excluded Scarborough and the Spratlys
timeline.description: Article III defined the ceded archipelago by coordinates; Scarborough Shoal and the Spratlys lie west of the treaty lines, which Beijing cites against Manila's claim and Manila answers with post-1946 practice and UNCLOS.
timeline.immediate_effect: US colonial rule of the Philippines until 1946.
timeline.long_term_effect: The treaty-limits argument recurs in PRC rebuttals; the Philippines abandoned treaty-line claims to maritime space when it adopted UNCLOS baselines in 2009.

timeline.name: France annexes Spratly features; Japan occupies both archipelagos
timeline.line: France annexes nine Spratly features; Japan takes the Spratlys and Paracels by 1939
timeline.description: France announced the annexation of nine Spratly features in 1933 and placed a garrison in the Paracels in 1938; Japan occupied both groups in 1939 and administered the Spratlys from Taiwan. The ROC protested the French move.
timeline.immediate_effect: First modern state occupation of the features.
timeline.long_term_effect: Vietnam's claim cites French administration as a predecessor title; the PRC and ROC cite their protests. Japan's wartime occupation set up the 1951 renunciation.

timeline.name: ROC publishes the eleven-dash line map
timeline.line: ROC government draws a dashed line around most of the South China Sea
timeline.description: After sending ships to take over the Japanese-held features in 1946, the ROC published an official map with an eleven-dash line (made public in early 1948). The PRC later removed two dashes in the Gulf of Tonkin. The line was never defined by coordinates and whether it claims islands only, historic waters, or rights over enclosed waters is contested, including within the PRC.
timeline.immediate_effect: No administration of the enclosed waters.
timeline.long_term_effect: The ambiguity survives in PRC 'historic rights' language and was the core issue the 2016 tribunal ruled on.

timeline.name: US-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty
timeline.line: US and Philippines sign a mutual defense treaty covering armed forces and public vessels in the Pacific
timeline.description: Article IV commits each party to act to meet an armed attack 'in accordance with its constitutional processes'; Article V includes attacks on armed forces, public vessels or aircraft in the Pacific. Since 2019 the US has stated this covers the South China Sea and the Philippine coast guard.
timeline.problem_solved: Cold War security guarantee for the newly independent Philippines.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, in force; its practical scope was clarified toward the South China Sea by US statements from 2019 onward.

timeline.name: Japan renounces the Spratlys and Paracels without naming a recipient
timeline.line: San Francisco treaty: Japan gives up the Spratlys and Paracels, but to no one
timeline.description: Article 2(f) renounced 'all right, title and claim' to the Spratly and Paracel Islands without assigning them. Neither the PRC nor the ROC was a party to the conference.
timeline.immediate_effect: Left sovereignty open to competing occupation.
timeline.long_term_effect: Every current claimant builds its case on pre-war history or post-war occupation because the settlement decided nothing.

timeline.name: ROC garrisons Itu Aba (Taiping) after Filipino 'Freedomland' claim
timeline.line: Taipei stations troops on Itu Aba, the largest natural Spratly feature
timeline.description: After Filipino adventurer Tomas Cloma proclaimed 'Freedomland' over part of the Spratlys in 1956, the ROC re-established a permanent garrison on Itu Aba, which it still holds.
timeline.immediate_effect: First continuous post-war occupation of a Spratly feature.
timeline.long_term_effect: Taiwan holds the largest natural Spratly island; the 2016 tribunal nevertheless classed Itu Aba as a rock for EEZ purposes, which Taipei also rejected.

timeline.name: PRC territorial sea declaration and Pham Van Dong's note
timeline.line: PRC declares a 12 nm sea including Xisha and Nansha; Hanoi's premier writes that he 'recognizes and supports' it
timeline.description: The PRC declaration named the Xisha and Nansha islands as Chinese. On 14 September Pham Van Dong wrote that the DRV recognized and supported the declaration. Beijing reads the note as acknowledgement of sovereignty; Hanoi argues it addressed only the 12 nm breadth, that the islands were then under RVN jurisdiction, and that wartime solidarity cannot alienate territory.
timeline.immediate_effect: None on the water; the islands were not under DRV control.
timeline.long_term_effect: A standing PRC argument against Vietnam's claim and the clearest example of a predecessor act whose meaning for the successor is disputed.

timeline.name: Battle of the Paracel Islands
timeline.line: PLA Navy defeats South Vietnam's navy and takes the whole Paracel group
timeline.description: A naval clash on 19 January 1974 followed by PLA landings gave the PRC control of the western Paracels held by the RVN; South Vietnamese losses were over 50 killed. The US, withdrawing from Vietnam and in rapprochement with Beijing, did not intervene.
timeline.immediate_effect: PRC control of all the Paracels.
timeline.long_term_effect: Unified Vietnam inherited the claim and the grievance; the Paracels are now the PRC's Sansha administrative base.

timeline.name: Socialist Republic of Vietnam proclaimed
timeline.line: Unified Vietnam inherits both the RVN's Spratly outposts and the DRV's 1958 note
timeline.description: After the fall of Saigon (April 1975), during which northern forces took the Spratly features held by the RVN, the DRV and the South were unified as the SRV.
timeline.immediate_effect: Vietnam asserted claims to both archipelagos, reversing Hanoi's wartime silence.
timeline.long_term_effect: Vietnam-PRC relations deteriorated to war in 1979; Vietnam today occupies the most Spratly features.

timeline.name: Philippines annexes the Kalayaan Island Group (PD 1596)
timeline.line: Marcos Sr. decrees most of the Spratlys a Philippine municipality
timeline.description: Presidential Decree 1596 declared the Kalayaan Island Group part of Philippine territory; RA 9522 (2009) later placed it under the UNCLOS regime of islands.
timeline.immediate_effect: Formalized Philippine occupation of Thitu and other features.
timeline.long_term_effect: The legal basis of the Philippine Spratly claim, distinct from its EEZ claim.

timeline.name: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea
timeline.line: UNCLOS creates 200 nm EEZs that overlap across the whole sea
timeline.description: Established the 200 nm EEZ, rules on islands versus rocks (Article 121) and compulsory dispute settlement (Part XV). All South China Sea littoral claimants ratified it (PRC 1996); the US has not ratified but says it observes the navigational rules as customary law.
timeline.problem_solved: Codified ocean zones and navigation rights.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, in force; the PRC made a 2006 Article 298 declaration excluding boundary delimitation from compulsory arbitration, which the 2016 tribunal held did not bar the Philippine case.

timeline.name: Johnson South Reef Skirmish
timeline.line: PLA Navy kills about 64 Vietnamese sailors and gains its first Spratly foothold
timeline.description: Chinese naval forces fired on Vietnamese personnel on Johnson South Reef; about 64 Vietnamese were killed. The PRC occupied six Spratly reefs that year. The USSR, Vietnam's ally, did not respond.
timeline.immediate_effect: First PRC presence in the Spratlys.
timeline.long_term_effect: The reefs taken in 1988 were among those turned into artificial islands after 2013.

timeline.name: PRC Law on the Territorial Sea names the Spratlys and Paracels
timeline.line: Beijing writes the Xisha and Nansha islands into national law
timeline.description: Article 2 lists the Dongsha, Xisha, Zhongsha and Nansha islands as PRC land territory.
timeline.immediate_effect: ASEAN issued its 1992 Manila Declaration urging restraint.
timeline.long_term_effect: Start of the pattern of consolidating claims through domestic legislation.

timeline.name: US forces leave Subic Bay
timeline.line: Last US forces leave the Philippines after the Senate rejects a base treaty
timeline.description: The Philippine Senate rejected a new bases treaty in September 1991; Clark had been abandoned after the Pinatubo eruption and the US Navy left Subic in November 1992. The MDT remained in force.
timeline.immediate_effect: No permanent US presence in the Philippines.
timeline.long_term_effect: The PRC occupied Mischief Reef about two years later; the causal link is argued by many analysts but not documented by Beijing.

timeline.name: Mischief Reef occupation
timeline.line: Philippines discovers PRC 'fishermen's shelters' on Mischief Reef inside its EEZ
timeline.description: Philippine patrols found PRC structures on the reef in February 1995; Beijing called them shelters for fishermen and expanded them into concrete structures in 1998-99. No shots were fired; Manila protested and sought ASEAN support.
timeline.immediate_effect: First PRC foothold near the Philippines; the Philippines grounded the Sierra Madre on nearby Second Thomas Shoal in 1999.
timeline.long_term_effect: Mischief Reef became one of the three large PRC airbase islands; the 2016 award held it is a low-tide elevation in the Philippine EEZ.

timeline.name: PRC declares straight baselines around the Paracels and ratifies UNCLOS
timeline.line: Beijing ratifies UNCLOS and draws archipelagic-style baselines it is not entitled to as a continental state
timeline.description: The PRC ratified UNCLOS and on the same day declared straight baselines enclosing the Paracels; the US and others hold that UNCLOS permits archipelagic baselines only for archipelagic states.
timeline.immediate_effect: Formal claim to internal waters inside the Paracels.
timeline.long_term_effect: Precedent for the November 2024 Scarborough baselines; a recurring target of US freedom of navigation operations.

timeline.name: US-Philippines Visiting Forces Agreement
timeline.line: Visiting Forces Agreement restores US rotational access after Subic
timeline.description: Set the legal status of US forces on temporary visits, enabling large exercises such as Balikatan.
timeline.problem_solved: Restored exercises and access without permanent bases.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes; Duterte gave termination notice in February 2020 and withdrew it in July 2021.

timeline.name: China-Vietnam Gulf of Tonkin delimitation agreement
timeline.line: Beijing and Hanoi agree a maritime boundary in the Gulf of Tonkin
timeline.description: Delimited territorial seas, EEZs and continental shelves in the Gulf, the only PRC maritime boundary agreed in the South China Sea area.
timeline.problem_solved: Fisheries and seabed disputes in the Gulf.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, in force; it covers only the Gulf and not the Paracels or Spratlys, showing Beijing will delimit where no island sovereignty is at stake.

timeline.name: EP-3 / J-8 collision off Hainan
timeline.line: A PLA fighter collides with a US surveillance plane; the crew is held 11 days
timeline.description: A PLA Navy J-8 collided with a US Navy EP-3 over the EEZ southeast of Hainan; the Chinese pilot died and the damaged EP-3 landed on Hainan. The 24 crew were released after a US letter expressing regret ('very sorry'), which the two sides translated differently.
timeline.immediate_effect: Crew released; aircraft returned in pieces.
timeline.long_term_effect: Crystallized the dispute over military activity in another state's EEZ, which the PRC contests and the US asserts.

timeline.name: ASEAN-China Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea
timeline.line: ASEAN and China sign a non-binding declaration to refrain from occupying uninhabited features
timeline.description: Paragraph 5 commits parties to self-restraint including 'refraining from action of inhabiting on the presently uninhabited islands, reefs, shoals, cays'. It is political, not legally binding, and envisaged a later code of conduct.
timeline.problem_solved: Froze new occupations of uninhabited features after the Mischief Reef crisis.
timeline.did_it_survive: Formally yes; no new uninhabited feature is known to have been occupied, but the 2013-2016 reclamation of already-held reefs, and Vietnam's later expansion, arguably breached its spirit. The binding code it anticipated had not been concluded by the July 2026 target.

timeline.name: USNS Impeccable harassment
timeline.line: PRC vessels swarm a US ocean-surveillance ship south of Hainan
timeline.description: Five PRC vessels, including fishing trawlers, closely shadowed and obstructed USNS Impeccable about 75 miles south of Hainan; the US protested and later sent a destroyer escort.
timeline.immediate_effect: Ship withdrew temporarily and resumed operations with escort.
timeline.long_term_effect: Early use of non-naval vessels to contest US military activity, a template for later militia tactics.

timeline.name: PRC submits the nine-dash-line map to the UN
timeline.line: Beijing attaches the nine-dash map to a UN note, internationalizing the line
timeline.description: Responding to the Malaysia-Vietnam joint continental shelf submission, the PRC note claimed 'indisputable sovereignty over the islands in the South China Sea and the adjacent waters' and attached the nine-dash-line map for the first time in a UN filing.
timeline.immediate_effect: Protests by Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia and (2011) the Philippines.
timeline.long_term_effect: Gave the Philippines the documentary basis to challenge the line's legality in 2013.

timeline.name: Reed Bank survey ship incident
timeline.line: PRC patrol boats order a Philippine-contracted survey ship off Reed Bank
timeline.description: Two PRC patrol vessels threatened a survey ship working for a Philippine concession at Reed Bank; the ship left and Philippine air assets arrived afterwards.
timeline.immediate_effect: Survey halted.
timeline.long_term_effect: Reed Bank remains undeveloped; energy exploration in contested blocks became a recurring trigger.

timeline.name: Scarborough Shoal standoff
timeline.line: PRC maritime agencies take effective control of Scarborough Shoal after a two-month standoff
timeline.description: A Philippine warship tried to arrest PRC fishermen; PRC maritime surveillance ships intervened. The Philippines withdrew its vessels in June; PRC vessels stayed. Accounts differ on whether a US-brokered mutual withdrawal was agreed and broken by Beijing or never agreed.
timeline.immediate_effect: PRC controls access to the lagoon.
timeline.long_term_effect: Triggered the Philippine arbitration filing in January 2013 and remains the shoal's status quo.

timeline.name: ASEAN fails to issue a communique; PRC establishes Sansha City
timeline.line: ASEAN foreign ministers fail to agree a communique for the first time; Beijing creates Sansha City to administer the claims
timeline.description: At Phnom Penh, chair Cambodia blocked references to Scarborough, and the meeting ended without a joint communique for the first time in ASEAN's history. Days later the PRC formally established the prefecture-level city of Sansha on Woody Island to administer the Paracels, Spratlys and Macclesfield Bank.
timeline.immediate_effect: Visible ASEAN division; permanent PRC civil administration of the claims.
timeline.long_term_effect: Consensus rules let a single member block collective positions; Sansha became the vehicle for later administrative districts (2020).

timeline.name: Philippines initiates UNCLOS arbitration
timeline.line: Manila takes Beijing to an UNCLOS tribunal; Beijing refuses to take part
timeline.description: The Philippines filed under UNCLOS Annex VII on the legality of the nine-dash line, the status of features and PRC conduct, avoiding sovereignty questions the tribunal could not hear. The PRC declined to participate.
timeline.immediate_effect: Tribunal constituted in 2013; PRC published a 2014 position paper on jurisdiction.
timeline.long_term_effect: Produced the 2016 award.

timeline.name: PRC artificial island-building in the Spratlys
timeline.line: PRC dredges about 3,200 acres of new land on seven Spratly reefs and builds three airfields
timeline.description: From late 2013 to 2016 the PRC reclaimed land on its seven Spratly reefs; Fiery Cross, Subi and Mischief received 3,000-metre runways, hangars, radars and later missile systems.
timeline.immediate_effect: Persistent PRC air and sea presence in the southern sea.
timeline.long_term_effect: Changed the military balance of the Spratlys in a way no ruling has reversed.

timeline.name: US-Philippines Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement
timeline.line: EDCA gives US forces rotational access to agreed Philippine bases
timeline.description: Allows US forces to preposition equipment and build facilities at agreed locations under Philippine ownership; upheld by the Philippine Supreme Court in 2016. Five sites were agreed in 2016 and four more in 2023, including in northern Luzon facing Taiwan.
timeline.problem_solved: US presence without permanent bases, which the 1987 constitution restricts.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, and expanded under Marcos Jr.

timeline.name: Haiyang Shiyou 981 oil rig standoff
timeline.line: PRC places a deep-water oil rig in waters claimed by Vietnam; rammings at sea, riots onshore
timeline.description: CNOOC's rig was positioned near the Paracels inside Vietnam's claimed EEZ with a large escort; Vietnamese and PRC vessels rammed and water-cannoned each other, a Vietnamese fishing boat was sunk, and anti-China riots in Vietnam killed several people. The rig was withdrawn in mid-July, a month earlier than announced.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rig withdrawn; Vietnam-PRC party channels used to calm the crisis.
timeline.long_term_effect: Vietnam deepened ties with the US, Japan and India while avoiding alliance.

timeline.name: Xi states China does not intend to militarize the Spratlys
timeline.line: At the White House, Xi says China 'does not intend to pursue militarization' of the Nansha islands
timeline.description: In a joint press conference Xi said construction in the Nansha islands did not target any country and China did not intend to pursue militarization; the outposts later received anti-ship and air-defense missiles, radars and military aircraft visits. Beijing describes these as defensive facilities on its own territory.
timeline.immediate_effect: Briefly eased US pressure.
timeline.long_term_effect: Cited by US officials as evidence that PRC verbal assurances on the sea do not constrain later action.

timeline.name: Arbitral award in Philippines v. China
timeline.line: UNCLOS tribunal rules PRC 'historic rights' within the nine-dash line have no legal basis
timeline.description: The tribunal found no legal basis for PRC historic rights to resources inside the nine-dash line, held that no Spratly feature generates an EEZ, classified Mischief Reef and Second Thomas Shoal as low-tide elevations in the Philippine EEZ, and found PRC reclamation and obstruction unlawful. It did not rule on sovereignty over land features.
timeline.immediate_effect: PRC declared the award 'null and void' with 'no binding force'; Duterte set it aside.
timeline.long_term_effect: The legal reference for Philippine law (RA 12064), US policy (2020) and most Western statements; unenforced on the water.

timeline.name: Duterte's pivot to Beijing
timeline.line: Duterte announces 'separation' from the US in Beijing and shelves the award
timeline.description: During a state visit Duterte announced separation from the US; Filipino fishermen regained access to Scarborough afterwards, and pledged PRC investment largely did not materialize.
timeline.immediate_effect: Reduced US-Philippine exercises and patrols.
timeline.long_term_effect: Reversed under Marcos Jr.; shows Philippine alignment swings with the president while the treaty persists.

timeline.name: PLA Navy seizes a US underwater drone
timeline.line: PLA Navy takes a US ocean glider near USNS Bowditch off Luzon, returns it five days later
timeline.description: A PLA Navy vessel recovered an unmanned glider being retrieved by USNS Bowditch about 50 nm northwest of Subic Bay; it was returned after US protests.
timeline.immediate_effect: Drone returned.
timeline.long_term_effect: Minor; illustrates quick resolution when neither side has sovereignty at stake.

timeline.name: USS Decatur near-collision at Gaven Reef
timeline.line: A PLA destroyer cuts within about 40 metres of a US destroyer on a freedom of navigation operation
timeline.description: During a FONOP near Gaven and Johnson reefs a PRC Luyang destroyer maneuvered within roughly 45 yards of USS Decatur's bow, forcing it to turn.
timeline.immediate_effect: No damage; protests exchanged.
timeline.long_term_effect: FONOPs continued; unsafe intercepts became a recurring US complaint.

timeline.name: Haiyang Dizhi 8 survey standoff at Vanguard Bank
timeline.line: PRC survey ship and escorts spend months in Vietnam's EEZ near a Vietnamese gas field
timeline.description: The survey vessel and CCG escorts operated near Vanguard Bank, where a Rosneft-operated rig worked under Vietnamese license, until October; Vietnamese vessels shadowed them.
timeline.immediate_effect: Survey ship withdrew; Vietnamese operations continued.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed Vietnam's preference for quiet shadowing and party-channel diplomacy over publicity.

timeline.name: US formally rejects PRC maritime claims
timeline.line: Washington aligns its policy with the 2016 award and calls Beijing's resource claims 'completely unlawful'
timeline.description: The Pompeo statement declared PRC claims to offshore resources across most of the sea unlawful and aligned US policy with the award, while still taking no position on sovereignty over land features. The 2022 Limits in the Seas No. 150 study set out the legal analysis.
timeline.immediate_effect: Shift from neutrality on maritime claims to explicit rejection.
timeline.long_term_effect: Maintained by subsequent administrations as of 2026.

timeline.name: PRC Coast Guard Law authorizes the use of weapons
timeline.line: Beijing's Coast Guard Law allows 'all necessary measures including the use of weapons' in PRC-claimed waters
timeline.description: Article 22 authorizes the CCG to use weapons when PRC sovereignty or jurisdiction is violated at sea by foreign organizations or individuals; Article 47 allows hand-held weapons. The law does not define the geographic scope of 'jurisdictional waters'. In force 1 February 2021.
timeline.immediate_effect: Protests from the Philippines, Vietnam and Japan.
timeline.long_term_effect: Legal basis for CCG boarding, water-cannon and blocking tactics used at Second Thomas and Scarborough.

timeline.name: Maritime militia massing at Whitsun Reef
timeline.line: About 220 PRC militia vessels moor at Whitsun Reef inside the Philippine EEZ
timeline.description: The Philippines reported some 220 PRC vessels at Whitsun Reef; Beijing said they were fishing boats sheltering from weather. Most dispersed across nearby Spratly features over the following weeks.
timeline.immediate_effect: Diplomatic protests; vessels dispersed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Brought the maritime militia into public view and influenced Manila's later transparency approach.

timeline.name: Vietnam accelerates Spratly reclamation
timeline.line: Vietnam's dredging expands its Spratly outposts, by 2024-25 approaching the PRC's reclaimed area
timeline.description: Satellite imagery tracked by AMTI showed Vietnam expanding land at many of its outposts from 2022, with large gains at Barque Canada Reef and others. Beijing has criticized it far more quietly than it criticizes Manila.
timeline.immediate_effect: More durable Vietnamese positions.
timeline.long_term_effect: Complicates the narrative that reclamation is a PRC-only practice; tests the 2002 DOC.

timeline.name: CCG water-cannons Philippine resupply at Second Thomas Shoal
timeline.line: CCG uses water cannon and blocking on Sierra Madre resupply missions through late 2023
timeline.description: Starting 5 August 2023 the CCG water-cannoned and blocked Philippine resupply boats, with collisions in October and further water-cannon use in December; Manila published video of each incident. Resupply mostly got through.
timeline.immediate_effect: US reiterated MDT coverage of Philippine coast guard vessels.
timeline.long_term_effect: Escalating pattern that led to the June 2024 clash.

timeline.name: June 2024 Second Thomas Shoal clash and provisional arrangement
timeline.line: CCG personnel with bladed weapons board Philippine boats; a sailor loses a thumb; talks yield a resupply arrangement
timeline.description: CCG personnel rammed, boarded and seized weapons from Philippine Navy boats resupplying the Sierra Madre, injuring several sailors. Manila chose not to invoke the MDT. Talks produced a 'provisional arrangement' announced 21 July, and the first resupply under it on 27 July passed without incident. The two sides describe its terms differently (PRC: advance notice, inspection, basic necessities only; Philippines: no permission-seeking).
timeline.immediate_effect: Uneventful resupply missions for a period.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed both governments would step back from a lethal threshold at this site; interpretation gap left the arrangement fragile.

timeline.name: Japan-Philippines Reciprocal Access Agreement
timeline.line: Japan and the Philippines sign a reciprocal access agreement for their forces
timeline.description: Allows each side's forces to deploy to the other for training and operations under agreed legal status; Japan's first such agreement in Asia. Entry into force is recorded here as September 2025 with moderate confidence.
timeline.problem_solved: Legal framework for Japan-Philippines exercises alongside the US.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, as of 2026; Japan joined US-Philippine maritime activity after the July 2026 clashes.

timeline.name: Sabina Shoal standoff
timeline.line: PCG cutter anchored at Sabina Shoal is rammed and withdraws after five months
timeline.description: The Philippine Coast Guard anchored BRP Teresa Magbanua at Sabina Shoal from April 2024 over suspected reclamation; CCG ships blockaded and rammed PCG vessels in August, and the cutter left on 14 September citing crew health and supplies. The CCG claimed it had forced the withdrawal.
timeline.immediate_effect: No Philippine ship permanently stationed; PCG patrols continued.
timeline.long_term_effect: Indicates the limits of a static outpost without resupply guarantees.

timeline.name: Philippine Maritime Zones Act and PRC Scarborough baselines
timeline.line: Manila legislates its maritime zones citing the arbitration; Beijing responds with baselines around Scarborough
timeline.description: RA 12064 declared Philippine maritime zones under UNCLOS and referenced PCA Case No. 2013-19. Within days the PRC declared territorial sea baselines around Scarborough Shoal, calling the law an attempt to 'solidify' the illegal award.
timeline.immediate_effect: Summons of envoys; competing domestic legal claims over the same shoal.
timeline.long_term_effect: Both sides' claims to Scarborough are now written into national law.

timeline.name: Scarborough Shoal pursuit and PRC ship collision
timeline.line: A PLA destroyer and a CCG cutter collide while chasing a Philippine patrol ship near Scarborough
timeline.description: While pursuing PCG cutter BRP Suluan, which was escorting aid to Filipino fishermen, PLA Navy destroyer Guilin struck CCG cutter 3104, badly damaging its bow. A month later Beijing designated a nature reserve at the shoal, and CCG water-cannon use against Philippine vessels there followed in September.
timeline.immediate_effect: No Philippine damage; PRC presence reinforced with an administrative measure.
timeline.long_term_effect: PLA Navy ships now join CCG pursuits at the shoal, raising accident risk.

timeline.name: PRC State Council approves a Huangyan Dao national nature reserve
timeline.line: Beijing declares a national nature reserve at Scarborough Shoal
timeline.description: The State Council approved a national nature reserve at Huangyan Dao, with area and zones to be announced by the National Forestry and Grassland Administration. Manila called the plan illegitimate and unlawful.
timeline.immediate_effect: Legal pretext for restricting access by other states' vessels.
timeline.long_term_effect: Another layer of domestic administration over a feature the award treats as a shared fishing ground.

timeline.name: ASEAN-China Code of Conduct misses its three-year target
timeline.line: The 2023 guidelines' July 2026 target for a Code of Conduct passes without a concluded text
timeline.description: The 2023 guidelines aimed to conclude a code within three years. Negotiations continued into 2026 (senior officials met in May; a working group met in Manila in September) with unresolved issues including legal bindingness and geographic scope; the parties now speak of concluding by year-end.
timeline.immediate_effect: Talks continue while incidents at sea continue.
timeline.long_term_effect: Unresolved; a code without binding force or defined scope would repeat the DOC's limits.

timeline.name: July 2026 clashes at Second Thomas and Scarborough shoals
timeline.line: Three China-Philippine clashes in a week; Philippine personnel injured at Second Thomas Shoal
timeline.description: On 20 July a CCG boat approached the Sierra Madre and at least one Philippine sailor was injured; Manila says Chinese personnel struck him with a baton, while Beijing says Philippine boats rammed first. On 24 July the CCG used water cannon on Philippine vessels supporting fishermen at Scarborough. The US condemned the actions; US, Japanese and Philippine forces held maritime activities and Marcos vowed not to yield the award.
timeline.immediate_effect: The 2024 arrangement's calm at Second Thomas Shoal broken; PRC protests against Manila.
timeline.long_term_effect: Unresolved as of September 2026.

territories.de_facto_control: country:PHL (the grounded ship), encircled by CCG and militia vessels
significance: most likely site of a lethal incident that could engage MDT Article IV

lessons.name: PRC: the 2016 award is null and void and will not be implemented
lessons.description: The PRC Foreign Ministry declared the award null and void with no binding force the day it was issued, and a State Council white paper the next day restated historic rights. Expect PRC conduct to ignore the award; this is stated policy, not inference.

lessons.name: US: MDT Article IV covers Philippine forces and coast guard in the South China Sea
lessons.description: US officials have stated since 2019 that an armed attack on Philippine armed forces, public vessels or aircraft, including the coast guard, anywhere in the South China Sea would invoke Article IV. Article IV still says 'in accordance with its constitutional processes', so what the US would actually do is not fixed; and Manila did not invoke the treaty after the June 2024 injuries.

lessons.name: PRC: consolidate control through law and administration below the armed-attack threshold
lessons.description: The literature widely describes a PRC approach of converting presence into legal-administrative facts (1992 law, 1996 baselines, Sansha 2012, 2021 Coast Guard Law, 2024 baselines, 2025 nature reserve) enforced by coast guard and militia rather than the navy. The pattern is well documented; calling it a deliberate 'grey zone strategy' is an outside interpretation.

lessons.name: ASEAN cannot act collectively against a member-state veto
lessons.description: The 2012 Phnom Penh failure and the non-binding 2002 DOC are commonly read as showing that ASEAN consensus lets a single member aligned with Beijing block collective positions, so claimants rely on bilateral deals and outside partners.

lessons.name: Vietnam: 'four nos' hedging, no alliances
lessons.description: Vietnam's 2019 defence white paper states no military alliances, no siding with one country against another, no foreign bases, and no use of force or threat of force in international relations. It explains why Vietnam shadows and protests quietly (2014, 2019) rather than seeking US guarantees.

lessons.name: Features changed hands when the defender's great-power backer was absent or disengaged
lessons.description: 1974 (US leaving Vietnam), 1988 (Soviet disengagement) and 1995 (three years after US forces left Subic) all fit this pattern, and no feature held by a US treaty ally's personnel has been taken since. This is an inference from three cases with other explanations (PRC naval capability growth, opportunity); it is not PRC doctrine.

tendencies.name: PRC converts incidents into lasting physical or administrative gains
current_evidence: After the August 2025 Scarborough collision Beijing added a nature reserve within a month; after Manila's 2024 Maritime Zones Act it declared Scarborough baselines within days.
tendencies.caveat: Beijing withdrew the 2014 oil rig and the 2019 survey ship without gains, accepted a 2024 arrangement that lets Philippine resupply continue, and has agreed a maritime boundary with Vietnam. Where it faced costs to wider relations it has stepped back; the ratchet is strongest where the counterpart is isolated.

tendencies.name: PRC keeps coercion non-lethal, led by coast guard and militia, since 1988
current_evidence: July 2026 incidents produced injuries but no reported deaths; June 2024 involved bladed weapons without firearms.
tendencies.caveat: Lethal force was used twice against isolated Vietnamese forces, the violence ceiling has risen (water cannon to ramming to boarding with blades to injuries), PLA Navy ships now join pursuits, and the 2021 Coast Guard Law authorizes weapons. A single accident could break the pattern without a policy decision.

tendencies.name: Philippine South China Sea policy swings with the president while alliance institutions persist
current_evidence: Marcos Jr. reversed Duterte's tilt, expanded EDCA and signed the Japan RAA, yet still negotiated the 2024 provisional arrangement with Beijing.
tendencies.caveat: The MDT was never abrogated, Duterte's VFA termination was withdrawn, and the armed forces and the arbitration remained constant across administrations. The next election (2028) could swing rhetoric more than institutions.

Occupations and seizures fill the vacuum (1956-1995)

2016 award rejects historic rights; PRC rejects the award
Current constraint: both sides have written Scarborough into domestic law (2024-2025), so neither government can concede without reversing its own statutes

path_dependencies.description: Each arrow is a hypothesis about causation; the documents exist, the causal weight of each link is an assessment.

path_dependencies.name: US presence in the Philippines: withdrawal, gap, return

chain.step: 1992 US leaves Subic; MDT remains without forces
1995 PRC occupies Mischief Reef
1998 VFA restores rotational exercises
2014 EDCA allows prepositioning; expanded 2023
Current constraint: US forces are rotational and at Philippine-owned sites, so US involvement in a shoal incident depends on the Article IV interpretation rather than a garrison

path_dependencies.description: The 1992-1995 link is a widely argued hypothesis, not established causation; the PRC has never linked Mischief Reef to the US withdrawal.

narratives.name: PRC: islands 'China's territory since ancient times'; the award as foreign interference
narratives.historical_event: Chinese fishing and navigation records; the 1946 recovery of Japanese-held features; the 1947 line
narratives.modern_interpretation: Official statements present sovereignty over the Nanhai Zhudao as established by history long before UNCLOS and the award as an illegitimate political manipulation encouraged by outside powers. The historical record of use is real; whether it amounts to sovereignty or rights over waters is the contested part.

narratives.name: Philippines: the 'West Philippine Sea' and the award as a won case being bullied away
narratives.modern_interpretation: Manila frames its EEZ as the West Philippine Sea, treats the award as final law now written into RA 12064, and publicizes CCG actions to cast the dispute as law versus force. Marcos invoked this directly in July 2026, saying Filipinos 'do not yield'. The framing leaves out the Philippines' own occupations and the Duterte years of setting the award aside.
