timeline.name: Qing cedes Taiwan to Japan (Treaty of Shimonoseki)
timeline.line: Qing cedes Taiwan to Japan after the First Sino-Japanese War
timeline.description: Article 2 ceded Taiwan and the Penghu islands to Japan in perpetuity after Qing defeat.
timeline.immediate_effect: Fifty years of Japanese rule.
timeline.long_term_effect: Both PRC and ROC narratives treat 1895 as a wound of the 'century of humiliation'; Taiwanese identity politics also trace to the colonial period.

timeline.name: ROC assumes control of Taiwan
timeline.line: ROC assumes control of Taiwan after Japan's surrender
timeline.description: ROC forces accepted the Japanese surrender on Taiwan. In the 1951 San Francisco treaty Japan renounced title to Taiwan without naming a recipient, which is the basis of the 'undetermined status' argument.
timeline.immediate_effect: Taiwan administered by the ROC.
timeline.long_term_effect: The legal ambiguity of 1945/1951 underlies competing sovereignty arguments today.

timeline.name: Chinese Civil War
timeline.line: Chinese Civil War ends with two governments across the Strait
timeline.description: The decisive 1946-49 phase ended with CCP victory on the mainland and the ROC government's relocation to Taipei in December 1949. No peace treaty or armistice was ever signed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Two governments each claiming to be China.
timeline.long_term_effect: The unresolved civil war is the legal frame the PRC uses for the Taiwan question; the ROC constitution still describes a mainland area.

timeline.name: PRC founded; ROC government relocates to Taipei
timeline.line: PRC proclaimed in Beijing; ROC government moves to Taipei
timeline.description: Mao proclaimed the PRC on 1 October 1949; the ROC government completed its move to Taipei in December.
timeline.immediate_effect: Separate governments across the Strait.
timeline.long_term_effect: The status quo the whole dispute is about.

timeline.name: First Taiwan Strait Crisis
timeline.line: First Strait crisis: PLA shells Kinmen, seizes the Yijiangshan islands
timeline.description: PLA artillery bombardment of Kinmen from September 1954; capture of Yijiangshan in January 1955; ROC evacuation of the Dachen islands with US help in February 1955. Congress passed the Formosa Resolution.
timeline.immediate_effect: US-ROC treaty and Formosa Resolution; PRC gained some coastal islands.
timeline.long_term_effect: Established the pattern of US commitment to Taiwan proper while leaving offshore islands ambiguous.

timeline.name: US-ROC Mutual Defense Treaty
timeline.line: US signs a defense treaty with the ROC during the first Strait crisis
timeline.description: Committed the US to defend Taiwan and Penghu (the offshore islands were covered only by the separate Formosa Resolution). Terminated by the US effective 1 January 1980 when recognition moved to Beijing.
timeline.problem_solved: Deterring PRC action during the 1954-55 crisis.
timeline.did_it_survive: No: abandoned by the US in 1979 for normalization with the PRC; replaced by the non-treaty Taiwan Relations Act.

timeline.name: Second Taiwan Strait Crisis
timeline.line: Second Strait crisis: intense bombardment of Kinmen, US escorts resupply
timeline.description: Heavy PLA bombardment of Kinmen from 23 August 1958; US naval escort of ROC resupply convoys; the bombardment settled into an odd-days pattern and faded without a change of control.
timeline.immediate_effect: No territorial change; US signalled it would not let Kinmen fall.
timeline.long_term_effect: Kinmen stayed ROC; the crisis is a precedent for coercion that stops short of invasion.

timeline.name: UN General Assembly Resolution 2758
timeline.line: UN seat passes to the PRC; ROC representatives expelled
timeline.description: Recognized PRC representatives as the only lawful representatives of China at the UN and expelled the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek. The text does not mention Taiwan; whether it settles Taiwan's status is contested between Beijing and Taipei/Washington.
timeline.immediate_effect: ROC lost its UN seat and most diplomatic recognition over the following decade.
timeline.long_term_effect: Foundation of the PRC's 'one China principle' in international organizations.

timeline.name: Shanghai Communique
timeline.line: US 'acknowledges' the one-China position of both sides
timeline.description: The US stated it 'acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain there is but one China' and did not challenge that position; it reaffirmed interest in a peaceful settlement.
timeline.immediate_effect: Opened US-PRC rapprochement.
timeline.long_term_effect: The wording ('acknowledges', not 'recognizes') is the basis of the US 'one China policy' as distinct from the PRC 'one China principle'.

timeline.name: US recognizes the PRC; Taiwan Relations Act enacted
timeline.line: US recognition shifts to Beijing; Taiwan Relations Act replaces the treaty
timeline.description: The US switched recognition on 1 January 1979 and terminated the 1954 treaty. Congress passed the Taiwan Relations Act (April 1979) requiring the US to provide Taiwan defensive arms and to maintain the capacity to resist force, without a defense commitment.
timeline.immediate_effect: Unofficial US-Taiwan relations; continued arms sales.
timeline.long_term_effect: The TRA is the legal source of US arms sales and of the deliberately ambiguous US commitment.

timeline.name: August 17 Communique and Six Assurances
timeline.line: US pledges to reduce arms sales gradually, while assuring Taipei
timeline.description: The US stated it did not seek a long-term policy of arms sales to Taiwan and would reduce them gradually, conditioned on the PRC's peaceful approach; simultaneously gave Taipei the Six Assurances (no end date, no consultation with Beijing, no mediation).
timeline.immediate_effect: Framework for arms sales that both sides read differently.
timeline.long_term_effect: Recurring PRC objection to each arms package cites this communique.

timeline.name: The '1992 Consensus'
timeline.line: The contested '1992 Consensus' becomes the KMT-Beijing basis for talks
timeline.description: Semi-official talks in Hong Kong in 1992 produced an understanding later labelled the '1992 Consensus' (a term coined in 2000). The KMT describes it as 'one China, respective interpretations'; Beijing omits the second half; the DPP denies a consensus existed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Basis for later KMT-era cross-strait engagement.
timeline.long_term_effect: Beijing conditions official contact on acceptance of it, which DPP governments refuse.

timeline.name: Third Taiwan Strait Crisis
timeline.line: Third Strait crisis: PLA missile tests around Taiwan's first direct election; US sends two carrier groups
timeline.description: After President Lee Teng-hui's June 1995 visit to Cornell, the PLA conducted missile tests and exercises in July-August 1995 and again in March 1996, bracketing Taiwan's first direct presidential election. The US deployed two carrier battle groups. Lee won; no clash occurred.
timeline.immediate_effect: Coercion failed to change the election; US demonstrated willingness to deploy.
timeline.long_term_effect: Widely read as the trigger for PLA investment in anti-access capabilities aimed at US carriers (interpretation, not PRC doctrine text).

timeline.name: PRC Anti-Secession Law
timeline.line: Anti-Secession Law codifies 'non-peaceful means' if Taiwan moves toward independence
timeline.description: Article 8 authorizes 'non-peaceful means' if 'Taiwan independence' forces cause secession, if major incidents entailing secession occur, or if possibilities for peaceful reunification are 'completely exhausted'.
timeline.immediate_effect: Domestic legal basis for force.
timeline.long_term_effect: Defines the declared triggers; the third trigger is open-ended and gives Beijing discretion.

timeline.name: DPP's Tsai Ing-wen elected; Beijing suspends official contact
timeline.line: DPP returns to power; Beijing cuts official channels over the 1992 Consensus
timeline.description: Tsai declined to endorse the 1992 Consensus; Beijing suspended official cross-strait communication mechanisms and resumed poaching diplomatic allies.
timeline.immediate_effect: Loss of eight ROC diplomatic allies during Tsai's terms.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set the pattern of pressure without dialogue that continued under Lai.

timeline.name: PLA exercises after the Pelosi visit
timeline.line: Largest PLA exercises to date encircle Taiwan after Speaker Pelosi's visit
timeline.description: After the US House Speaker visited Taipei on 2-3 August 2022, the PLA held live-fire exercises in seven zones around Taiwan, fired ballistic missiles over the island (several landing in Japan's EEZ), and normalized crossings of the median line afterwards.
timeline.immediate_effect: Beijing suspended several dialogue channels with Washington.
timeline.long_term_effect: Median-line crossings and larger daily air activity became routine; the exercise template was reused in 2023-2025.

timeline.name: Joint Sword exercise after the Tsai-McCarthy meeting
timeline.line: Joint Sword: three-day encirclement drill after Tsai meets the US House Speaker in California
timeline.description: Three days of joint exercises simulating encirclement and precision strikes, smaller than August 2022.
timeline.immediate_effect: None beyond signalling.
timeline.long_term_effect: Confirmed the trigger-response pattern.

timeline.name: Joint Sword-2024A after Lai's inauguration
timeline.line: Joint Sword-2024A three days after President Lai's inauguration
timeline.description: Two-day drills described by the PLA as 'punishment' for 'separatist acts', including coast guard participation around Taiwan's outlying islands.
timeline.immediate_effect: None beyond signalling.
timeline.long_term_effect: Coast guard integration pointed toward quarantine-style options.

timeline.name: Joint Sword-2024B after Lai's National Day speech
timeline.line: Joint Sword-2024B: one-day drill with a record aircraft count, rehearsing port blockade
timeline.description: A single-day exercise with a record number of PLA aircraft recorded by Taiwan's MND, with stated focus on sealing key ports.
timeline.immediate_effect: None beyond signalling.
timeline.long_term_effect: Shorter-notice, port-focused drills raised concern about a blockade or quarantine scenario.

timeline.name: Strait Thunder-2025A
timeline.line: Strait Thunder-2025A: unannounced drills with stated focus on blockading ports and energy
timeline.description: Unannounced two-day exercises including simulated strikes on ports and energy infrastructure and live-fire in the East China Sea.
timeline.immediate_effect: None beyond signalling.
timeline.long_term_effect: Energy-interdiction emphasis matches Taiwan's LNG dependence.

lessons.name: PRC: formal independence is a defined trigger for force
lessons.description: The Anti-Secession Law and successive party congress reports state that the PRC will not renounce the use of force and define secession as a trigger. This is written policy, not inference.

lessons.name: US: keep the commitment ambiguous to deter both sides
lessons.description: The TRA commits the US to arms sales and capacity, not to defense. Analysts call the resulting posture 'strategic ambiguity'; the phrase is an interpretation, and several presidents have made statements at odds with it.

lessons.name: PLA: deny US carriers access after 1996
lessons.description: The standard interpretation of post-1996 PLA modernization is that the US carrier deployment taught Beijing to invest in anti-ship missiles, submarines and air defense. PRC documents do not state this causal link; it is inferred by outside analysts.

lessons.name: ROC: asymmetric, survivable defense (Overall Defense Concept)
lessons.description: Taiwan's 2017 Overall Defense Concept prioritized mobile, dispersed, numerous cheap systems over prestige platforms. Its full adoption is disputed within Taiwan's military, so the doctrine is documented but its implementation is contested.

tendencies.name: PRC responds to political triggers with demonstrations kept below the conflict threshold
current_evidence: Each exercise since 2022 has ended within days with no strike or blockade, while the baseline of daily air and naval activity has ratcheted upward afterwards.
tendencies.caveat: The pre-1979 cases involved real bombardment and island seizures; a leadership that judged the political or military balance had shifted could break the post-1995 pattern. Recency does not make the pattern a law.

path_dependencies.name: From 1949 to today's constraint set

chain.step: 1949 civil war ends without settlement
1971 UN seat and 1979 US recognition move to Beijing
Taiwan Relations Act institutionalizes arms sales without a defense pledge
2005 Anti-Secession Law codifies force triggers
Current constraint: a formal independence declaration is a declared PRC trigger; US response is legally discretionary; Taiwan's leaders campaign on 'status quo'

path_dependencies.description: Each arrow is a hypothesis about causation; the documents exist, the causal weight of each is an assessment.

narratives.name: PRC: reunification as part of national rejuvenation
narratives.modern_interpretation: Party documents frame 'complete reunification' as a requirement of the 'great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation' and cast the century of humiliation as the wound being healed. The narrative is documented; whether it sets a timetable is an inference.

narratives.name: Taiwan: the ROC/Taiwan is already sovereign; no need to declare independence
narratives.modern_interpretation: DPP governments hold that Taiwan is already a sovereign state under the ROC name, so 'maintaining the status quo' is the policy; the KMT frames the same status quo through the 1992 Consensus. Both are political positions layered on the same facts.

coercive_military_demonstration.selection_note: Cases are PRC military demonstrations around Taiwan following a political trigger. The set is complete for named Strait crises and named PLA exercise series since 1954 but omits routine ADIZ incursions, so it measures how named crises ended, not day-to-day pressure. Pre-1979 cases occurred before US-PRC normalization and before PRC nuclear/missile parity; weight them accordingly.
